title: Role of the Nurse in Promoting Nutrition for Inpatients

headings.title: Introduction to Inpatient Nutritional Care
headings.content:
Good nutrition is a cornerstone of patient recovery in the hospital setting. When patients are admitted, their bodies often face increased metabolic demands due to surgery, trauma, or infection. Inpatient nutritional care goes beyond simply serving meals; it is a clinical intervention aimed at preventing malnutrition, preserving lean muscle mass, and supporting wound healing and immune function.

Hospitalized patients are at high risk for malnutrition due to illness, fasting for tests, poor appetite, and unfamiliar food. Nurses interact with patients more frequently than any other healthcare provider, placing them in the ideal position to observe eating habits, identify early signs of nutritional decline, and advocate for timely dietary support. Recognizing nutrition as a vital sign ensures that clinical care addresses both the disease process and the patient's underlying nutritional needs.

headings.title: Nutritional Screening and Assessment on Admission
headings.content:
Identifying patients who are malnourished or at risk must happen promptly upon admission. Nurses usually perform the initial **nutritional screening** using validated tools that look at recent weight loss, body mass index, and acute disease severity. 

If a screen flags a patient as high risk, a comprehensive **nutritional assessment** follows, often completed by a registered dietitian. The nurse's role in this process involves:
- **Weight measurement**: Obtaining an accurate baseline weight using the same scale whenever possible.
- **Height estimation**: Measuring height directly rather than relying on patient recall, which is often inaccurate.
- **History collection**: Documenting recent changes in clothing fit, appetite, and swallowing difficulties.
- **Skin integrity check**: Observing for signs of micronutrient deficiencies or breakdown risks.

headings.title: Collaborating with Dietitians and the Healthcare Team
headings.content:
Nutritional care is never a solo effort. Effective inpatient management relies heavily on close communication between nurses, registered dietitians, physicians, speech-language pathologists, and pharmacists.

| Team Member | Primary Nutritional Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| **Registered Dietitian (RD)** | Calculates exact calorie and protein needs; prescribes specialized medical diets. |
| **Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP)** | Evaluates swallowing safety and recommends appropriate food textures. |
| **Pharmacist** | Reviews medications for potential nutrient-drug interactions or absorption issues. |
| **Bedside Nurse** | Observes daily intake, reports feeding struggles, and ensures diet orders are followed. |

Nurses serve as the central hub for this team. Because nurses spend the most time at the bedside, they are the first to notice if a diet order is too difficult for a patient to chew or if a supplement is consistently left untouched.

headings.title: Assisting with Feeding and Mealtime Management
headings.content:
Serving a meal tray is only the first step of mealtime management. Many inpatients experience physical weakness, confusion, visual impairments, or paralysis that makes independent eating impossible. 

Creating a calm, clean environment before the meal tray arrives significantly improves intake. Nurses and assistive personnel should clear bedside tables of clutter, ensure the patient's hands are washed, and position the patient upright at a 90-degree angle to prevent choking. Dentures, eyeglasses, and hearing aids should be in place.

When actively feeding a patient, never rush the process. Offer small, manageable bites, alternate between solids and liquids, and allow adequate time for chewing and swallowing. For patients with cognitive impairment, simple verbal cues or gentle hand-over-hand guidance can encourage self-feeding and preserve dignity.

headings.title: Monitoring Dietary Intake and Hydration Status
headings.content:
Accurate documentation of what a patient actually eats and drinks is essential for evaluating nutritional therapy. In many facilities, nurses use **percentage estimation** to record meal intake—estimating whether the patient consumed 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of their meal.

Fluid balance requires equal diligence. Nurses must track all fluid intake (oral liquids, IV fluids, tube flushes) and output (urine, liquid stool, drains) meticulously. A common clinical error is assuming that a full meal tray was eaten simply because it was returned empty, when in reality, food may have been spilled or eaten by a visitor. 

Signs of dehydration—such as poor skin turgor, concentrated dark urine, dry mucous membranes, and sudden weight drops—must be reported immediately to prevent acute kidney injury.

headings.title: Managing Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition Support
headings.content:
When oral intake is impossible or insufficient, patients may require artificial nutrition. 

**Enteral nutrition** (tube feeding) delivers liquid nutrients directly into the stomach or small intestine via a nasogastric, gastrostomy, or jejunostomy tube. The nurse's primary responsibilities include verifying tube placement before giving formulas or medications, checking residual volumes as ordered, elevating the head of the bed to at least 30 to 45 degrees during feeds to prevent aspiration, and flushing the tube regularly to prevent clogging.

**Parenteral nutrition** delivers specialized nutrient solutions directly into the bloodstream through a central venous catheter. Because parenteral solutions contain high concentrations of glucose and amino acids, they serve as a breeding ground for bacteria. Nurses must maintain strict aseptic technique during tubing and filter changes, monitor blood glucose levels frequently, and inspect the insertion site for signs of infection.

headings.title: Patient and Family Education on Nutrition
headings.content:
Nutritional care does not end at hospital discharge. Preparing patients to manage their own dietary needs at home is a vital nursing duty. Education must be tailored to the patient's cultural background, financial resources, cooking skills, and health literacy level.

Instead of handing out generic printed pamphlets, nurses should engage patients and their families in practical discussions. For example, a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure needs clear, concrete guidance on reading food labels for sodium content rather than just a warning to "eat less salt." Demonstrating how to modify favorite cultural dishes to meet therapeutic restrictions increases compliance and promotes long-term health. Involving family members who prepare meals ensures that the patient has a reliable support system after leaving the hospital.

headings.title: Evaluating Outcomes and Documenting Nutritional Care
headings.content:
Evaluating the success of nutritional interventions closes the clinical loop. Nurses monitor clinical markers such as steady weight trends, improved energy levels, normal laboratory values (like serum albumin and prealbumin when indicated), and clean, healing surgical wounds.

Accurate documentation creates a permanent legal record of the patient's nutritional journey and interprofessional collaboration. Nurses must chart specific details: meal intake percentages, tube feeding tolerances, daily weights, patient weight changes, and any specialized education provided. Thorough charting protects the patient's safety, ensures continuity of care across shifts, and validates the clinical necessity of ongoing nutritional support.
